questions.title: Primary manifestation of acute iron toxicity
questions.question: Which of the following is a primary manifestation of acute iron toxicity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haemochromatosis is a chronic iron-overload condition (organ iron deposition over years), not the acute manifestation of a single toxic ingestion.
explanations.B: Correct. Acute iron toxicity (classically from accidental ingestion of iron tablets, especially in children) primarily damages the gastrointestinal mucosa, producing necrotizing gastroenteritis as its primary manifestation. Corrosive injury to the gut lining causes vomiting, abdominal pain and gastrointestinal bleeding, which can progress to systemic toxicity (metabolic acidosis, shock, hepatic injury) if untreated.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute iron toxicity tends toward metabolic acidosis as toxicity progresses, not respiratory alkalosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypotension and shock (from fluid loss and direct cardiotoxicity), not hypertension, are features of severe iron toxicity.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Tachycardia (from hypovolaemia and shock), not bradycardia, is the expected cardiovascular finding in significant iron toxicity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify necrotizing gastroenteritis as the primary manifestation of acute iron toxicity.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.146

questions.title: Antidote for decontamination in acute iron toxicity
questions.question: What is the specific antidote used for decontamination in acute iron toxicity?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Deferasirox is an oral iron chelator used for chronic iron overload (as in repeated transfusions), not the specific decontamination antidote for acute iron poisoning.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dimercaprol is a chelator used for arsenic, mercury and lead poisoning, not iron.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Penicillamine is a chelator used mainly for copper (Wilson's disease) and sometimes lead, not iron.
explanations.D: Correct. Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine), an iron-chelating agent, binds free iron and allows its excretion, and is the specific antidote used for decontamination in acute iron toxicity. It is given parenterally in significant poisoning to bind circulating free iron before it causes further tissue damage.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Flumazenil is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose, unrelated to iron toxicity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify desferrioxamine as the specific antidote for acute iron toxicity decontamination.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.146

questions.title: Poisoning treated by hydroxocobalamin
questions.question: A therapeutic use of Vitamin B12 (specifically hydroxocobalamin) is in the treatment of which type of poisoning?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lead poisoning is treated with chelators such as dimercaprol, EDTA, or succimer, not hydroxocobalamin.
explanations.B: Correct. Hydroxocobalamin, a form of vitamin B12, given in high dose, is a specific antidote for cyanide poisoning. Its cobalt centre binds free cyanide ion with high affinity, converting it into cyanocobalamin (a stable, non-toxic B12 form) that is excreted renally — removing cyanide from mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, where it would otherwise block the electron transport chain and cause cellular asphyxiation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Arsenic poisoning is treated with dimercaprol, not hydroxocobalamin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Iron poisoning is treated with desferrioxamine, not hydroxocobalamin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Carbon monoxide poisoning is treated with 100% oxygen (or hyperbaric oxygen), not hydroxocobalamin.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hydroxocobalamin as the specific antidote for cyanide poisoning, distinct from its role in treating B12 deficiency.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.147

questions.title: Dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor causing folate-responsive anemia
questions.question: Folic acid can be used therapeutically to alleviate anemia associated with dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors. Which of the following is an example of such a drug?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Phenytoin can reduce folate levels through altered absorption/metabolism, but it does not act as a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Oral contraceptives are not dihydrofolate reductase inhibitors.
explanations.C: Correct. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), the enzyme that regenerates active tetrahydrofolate — its anticancer and immunosuppressive action comes from starving rapidly dividing cells of active folate. This same mechanism, applied systemically, can also produce a folate-deficiency-pattern (megaloblastic) anaemia as an adverse effect, which is why folinic acid (leucovorin, a folate form that bypasses the DHFR block) is given as rescue therapy in high-dose methotrexate regimens.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Erythropoietin stimulates red cell production directly; it is not a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Iron dextran is a parenteral iron preparation, not a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor.

questions.learning_objective: Identify methotrexate as a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor whose mechanism can produce a folate-deficiency-pattern anaemia.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.148

questions.title: Diagnosis in a vignette of macrocytic anemia with neurological symptoms
questions.question: A 63-year-old woman came to the clinic because of tiredness. She has been increasingly fatigued over the past year but in recent weeks has become breathless on exertion. Her feet have become numb and she has started to become unsteady on her feet. Her lab investigations showed Haemoglobin 8.2 g/dL (normal 11.7-15.7 g/dL) and Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) 112 fL (normal 80-99 fL). What is the most probable diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anaemia of chronic disease is typically normocytic or mildly microcytic, not markedly macrocytic (raised MCV) as in this vignette.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Haemolytic anaemia does not typically present with the described neurological symptoms (numbness, unsteady gait), and while it can raise MCV modestly via reticulocytosis, it does not fit this vignette's overall picture as well as megaloblastic anaemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Iron deficiency anaemia produces a microcytic, not macrocytic, picture — the opposite MCV direction from what is described here.
explanations.D: Correct. The combination of anaemia, a markedly raised MCV (macrocytosis, 112 fL against a normal upper limit of 99 fL), and neurological symptoms (numbness, unsteady gait/ataxia) points to megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 deficiency. Folate deficiency causes an identical megaloblastic blood picture, but only B12 deficiency produces this kind of neurological involvement, which is the key discriminator in this vignette.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise macrocytic anaemia with neurological symptoms as pointing to megaloblastic (B12-deficiency) anaemia.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.147 (vignette continues to p.148)

questions.title: Cause of the neurological manifestation in the B12-deficiency vignette
questions.question: Neurological manifestation in this patient is due to:

options.E: Subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord

explanations.A: Incorrect. Autonomic neuropathy affects the autonomic nervous system (blood pressure, bowel/bladder control), not the sensory ataxia and upper motor neuron pattern described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a focal median nerve compression at the wrist, an unrelated, localised condition.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Diabetic neuropathy is a plausible cause of peripheral numbness in an older patient, but nothing in this vignette suggests diabetes, and the combination with megaloblastic anaemia points specifically to B12 deficiency's own neurological complication instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Peripheral neuritis is a nonspecific term for peripheral nerve inflammation, not the specific named complication of B12 deficiency this vignette is testing.
explanations.E: Correct. Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord is B12 deficiency's specific neurological complication — a demyelination of the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts that produces the characteristic combination of impaired proprioception/vibration sense (unsteady gait, numbness) and upper motor neuron signs. It is the mechanistic link between this patient's megaloblastic anaemia and her neurological symptoms.

questions.learning_objective: Name subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord as B12 deficiency's specific neurological complication.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter beside option, p.148 (continuation of the p.147 vignette)

questions.title: Vignette of atrophic gastritis with hypersegmented neutrophils
questions.question: A 60-year-old patient presented with anorexia, weakness, paresthesia and mental changes. His tongue was red, tendon reflexes were diminished, hemoglobin was 6 g% with large red cells and neutrophils had hypersegmented nuclei. Endoscopy revealed atrophic gastritis. Supplementation of which factor is likely to correct his condition?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Folic acid would correct the anaemia but not the atrophic-gastritis mechanism or the neurological findings, and could mask ongoing B12-deficiency neurological damage if given alone.
explanations.B: Correct. Pernicious anaemia is vitamin B12 deficiency caused by autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells (and the intrinsic factor they secrete), producing the atrophic gastritis seen on endoscopy. The vignette's B12-specific findings — glossitis (red tongue), diminished reflexes, paraesthesia, mental changes, and hypersegmented neutrophils (six or more nuclear lobes, reflecting impaired DNA synthesis in the myeloid line as well as the erythroid line) — together with the large red cells (macrocytosis) point specifically to vitamin B12 supplementation as the corrective treatment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiency causes a sideroblastic-pattern anaemia, not this megaloblastic, atrophic-gastritis picture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency is not associated with this vignette's findings.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Iron supplementation would not address this patient's macrocytic, hypersegmented-neutrophil, atrophic-gastritis presentation, which points to B12 deficiency rather than iron deficiency (which would instead show microcytic red cells).

questions.learning_objective: Recognise atrophic gastritis with hypersegmented neutrophils as the pernicious-anaemia vignette, corrected by vitamin B12.
